title: Tool Invocation & Constrained-Decode Performance Sync
next_steps: Marcus to run constrained-decode microbenchmarks and share results
Schedule on-prem VPC benchmark in Nova test lane
Send latency-by-token spreadsheet and recommended configs
action_items: Marcus Chen: run constrained-decode benchmark (8k context, batch sizes 1/4/16), due 2025-03-25
Priya Patel: provide representative prompt set and top-3 tool schemas by 2025-03-21
Lena Ortega: share security and VPC checklist + sample private-deploy runbook by 2025-03-20
summary: Deep dive on runtime impact of function/tool invocation and structured JSON mode (constrained decoding). Discussed where overhead comes from (token rejection, regen loops, KV cache interactions), mitigation paths (prefixing, lexicon WFSA, model variant routing, batching heuristics) and agreed to run microbenchmarks in both hosted and VPC/on-prem lanes. SE to produce numbers and a config recommendation spreadsheet.
topics: KV cache interactions with partial generation
transcript: 00:00:00 Lena: ok starting now, thanks everyone for joining, we wanna focus on the tool invocation and json constrained mode perf today 00:00:08 Dana: yeah thanks, we got a handful of customers pushing structured outputs so latency matters a lot 00:00:12 Marcus: quick introductions? I’m Marcus, infra runtime SE at Redwood, I’ll be running the microbenchmarks 00:00:18 Priya: Priya Patel, ML engineering at Nova, mostly responsible for agent orchestration and prompt infra 00:00:23 Omar: Omar Ruiz, infra - I own the VPC/on-prem pipeline and the connecting peering 00:00:27 Lena: great, quick agenda — where overhead shows up, KV cache effects, batching interplay, quantization/compilers, and then ops for VPC tests 00:00:35 Priya: can we start with the observable symptom? our app is seeing 3x token latency when we enable json-mode strict output 00:00:42 Marcus: that’s believable — constrained decoding often forces the model into rejection/regeneration loops when tokens don’t match the allowed DFA or schema, so you see extra decoding iterations 00:00:52 Priya: are those re-gens happening because of top-k sampling randomness or because of the constraint enforcement algorithm? 00:00:58 Marcus: a mix — if you use a hard-constrain approach that edits the token distribution each step to zero-out disallowed tokens, you can still get low-probability tokens near the boundary and occasionally the model picks something that violates a later constraint, then our post-check rejects and we rewind or force a different path. That causes extra per-request decode time 00:01:16 Omar: rewind meaning we throw away generated tokens and re-decode from last checkpoint? does that flush the KV cache? 00:01:22 Marcus: good question — in our runtime we try to reuse KV cache as much as possible. Small rewinds (like backtracking one or two tokens) can still leverage cache; big re-rolls can degrade because we need to replay generation steps. But there are cases where the runtime invalidates chunked cache entries, so throughput suffers 00:01:39 Priya: we’re seeing spikes when our tool schema has nested arrays and keys with variable order — maybe the validator is too strict 00:01:45 Marcus: validators and schema determinism matter. If you can canonicalize ordering or prefer name-based keys, that reduces the combinatorial space the constrained decoder needs to explore 00:01:55 Lena: note — Redwood has two constrained strategies: token masking (hard filter) and WFSA-style lexicon constraints. Masking is cheaper per-token but leads to more rejects; WFSA is heavier per-step but fewer re-rolls overall 00:02:07 Dana: WFSA—uh is that the finite automaton approach? does that mean compiling the schema into a state machine? 00:02:11 Marcus: yes exactly, we compile the grammar into a compact automaton that can be traversed with dynamic programming. It’s costlier to set up but reduces the extra decode loops because it reasons across tokens 00:02:22 Omar: setup meaning CPU work at the start of request — does that add to tail latency? 00:02:25 Marcus: a little — usually single-digit ms for small schemas, but with huge nested grammars it can be 20-30ms extra. Compare that to 50-300ms from regen loops and it's often worth it 00:02:38 Priya: what about batching? we batch at 8 but when we enable json-mode the p99 jumps 00:02:44 Marcus: batching amplifies the problem — constrained decoding is hard to batch efficiently because different requests may be in different automaton states. Continuous batching strategies can group similar-state requests but complexity increases. For strict low-latency we often recommend batch size 1 or very small batch sizes and use batching only for throughput endpoints 00:03:03 Omar: on our side, the VPC adds 7-12ms of north-south latency to the control plane for hosted function calls — is that expected? 00:03:10 Marcus: yes that's plausible — plus if you’re calling external tools via webhooks from within the model output loop, those external network calls dominate. We recommend avoiding synchronous tool calling in the token loop where possible 00:03:21 Priya: our agent uses function-calling to hit an internal inventory service. If the model tries to call the function in the middle of generation and we wait, that stalls the whole token stream 00:03:30 Marcus: exactly — pattern advice: let the model emit a structured intent (call-name + args) then do the external call outside the critical token path and feed results back as a new prompt or cached context 00:03:41 Dana: that’s a change in design but doable. Will that change user perceived latency? 00:03:45 Marcus: you might see slightly higher end-to-end latency for the user-perceived action but much lower tail latency for the generation pipeline; plus it avoids regen loops triggered by runtime timeouts 00:03:57 Lena: what about quantization and kernel compilation — any effects on constrained decode? 00:04:02 Marcus: quantization reduces per-token compute but can increase variability in token probabilities, which sometimes leads to more margin errors with strict constraints. Also, some kernels are optimized for dense softmax ops but not for sparse masking — when you mask many tokens you break vectorized paths and fall back to slower loops 00:04:20 Priya: so using int8 q8_a vs q4_0 could change how often we hit re-rolls? 00:04:25 Marcus: yes partially — lower-precision sometimes flattens the distribution causing more ambiguity at token boundaries. We table results in the spreadsheet for different quant modes 00:04:34 Omar: for our private deployment we run on A100 and want to quantize for cost — any recommended profiles? 00:04:39 Marcus: recommend trying block q8 first for on-prem; pair that with kernel builds that support masked softmax and per-head scaling. Also use a shorter compilation target if you plan to switch kernels often 00:04:49 Priya: can KV cache help constrained decoding? like caching prefixes to avoid regen cost? 00:04:54 Marcus: great point — prefix/KV caching helps when you have repeated sub-prompts or tool responses; if regen means you replay the same prefix many times, a warm KV cache avoids recomputing key/value projections. But note: if regen rewrites the prefix content, caches may be invalidated 00:05:10 Priya: our agent sometimes inserts tool outputs as inline JSON, which changes the prefix length a lot 00:05:15 Marcus: that can evict cache slices and hurt throughput. One trick is to store tool outputs as external references and only materialize them in the prompt when necessary 00:05:26 Dana: can you explain the heuristic routing you mentioned earlier? 00:05:29 Marcus: routing by SLO: we tag requests that require strict-json with a low-latency lane—small batches, WFSA, maybe a slightly larger model to reduce rejects. Requests that are tolerant use larger batching and cheaper masking. Auto-fallback to a permissive mode is also an option 00:05:44 Priya: slightly larger model to reduce rejects — that increases token compute though 00:05:48 Marcus: true but it can be cheaper if it avoids multiple regen passes. There’s a crossover point where a single pass on bigger model costs less than several passes on smaller one 00:05:58 Lena: tradeoffs — compute cost vs wall-clock latency vs reliability. Our optimize tooling can simulate these with your prompt set 00:06:06 Omar: on hardware warmup — cold model startup in private deployments adds 200-400ms we noticed 00:06:12 Marcus: cold start kills p99. For private fleets, pin a small pool of warm seats for low-latency lanes or use a tiny warm model snapshot to handle constrained-decode critical traffic 00:06:23 Priya: what about streaming? we stream tokens but when constraint fails mid-stream what’s the UX? 00:06:28 Marcus: streaming with constraints is tricky — if you stream partial tokens and then the output is rejected, you can either emit a correction chunk or close + restart. Many customers prefer the model to emit a single structured block at the end when strict correctness matters 00:06:42 Dana: that hurts real-time feel though 00:06:45 Marcus: it's a tradeoff again 00:06:47 Lena: practical recommendations we’re proposing: 1) canonicalize schemas, 2) prefer WFSA for strict endpoints, 3) use small batches for strict lanes, 4) warm KV cache and avoid inline large tool outputs, 5) test quant profiles with regen-aware benchmarks 00:07:06 Priya: can you show actual numbers? 00:07:08 Marcus: yes — I ran quick microbench earlier: baseline free-gen token latency 20ms/token (A100, q8), with masking constraints it jumps to ~45-60ms/token due to rejects, with WFSA down to ~28-35ms/token. End-to-end p95 for our sample prompt set: baseline 420ms, masking 1.8s, WFSA 680ms (these are rough numbers) 00:07:32 Omar: where does network factor? if we include VPC add-on and webhook latency it pushes p95 over 2.4s in our tests 00:07:39 Marcus: yes external sync calls are dominant 00:07:42 Priya: these numbers would be super helpful — can you attach the raw runs? 00:07:45 Marcus: will attach the spreadsheet — link sent in deck 00:07:48 Lena: on the topic of function calling: does Redwood run the function-decoder logic inside the runtime or as post-processing? 00:07:55 Marcus: in hosted mode we do token-level enforcement inside the runtime for tight integrations. For private deployments customers can choose runtime vs post-processing models — runtime lowers roundtrip but increases complexity for constrained decoding 00:08:08 Priya: so in our VPC we might want to offload function execution to our infra after the model emits an intent 00:08:13 Omar: that matches our security posture — prefer control of external I/O 00:08:17 Marcus: for that path we can optimize by returning the intent only, and then you call back with a sanitized summary to the model as new context 00:08:27 Dana: about rate limiting and quotas — do constrained endpoints cost more? 00:08:32 Marcus: cost per token might be same, but effective cost per successful structured response can be 2-5x when many re-rolls happen. Our billing has a breakdown token vs regen multiplier in the console 00:08:44 Priya: any settings we should try right away? 00:08:47 Marcus: try switching to WFSA for your top-5 schemas, reduce batch from 8 to 1 for the strict path, and test q8 vs q4 to see regen differences. Also canonicalize keys and prefer string enums when possible 00:09:02 Omar: for on-prem kernel builds — anything we must enable? masked softmax, per-head scaling, and a patch for contiguous kv layout helped us 00:09:10 Marcus: yep those are the main ones. Also ensure your runtime uses fused attention kernels for long context 00:09:15 Priya: how do we benchmark regen-friendly prompts? 00:09:19 Marcus: we’ll provide a harness — it's basically many variants of the prompt set with slight perturbations in formatting, random seeds, and different tool outputs to exercise backtracking 00:09:29 Lena: we should recap next steps — Marcus will run full microbench in hosted and VPC lanes with the provided prompt set, priya will share prompts and schemas, lena shares ops docs 00:09:40 Dana: ok thanks, one last question — if we need absolute determinism can Redwood guarantee deterministic outputs in constrained mode? 00:09:47 Marcus: constrained WFSA with greedy decoding can be deterministic, but you pay in quality and you lose stochastic creativity. We can lock seeds and force greedy but it's a different mode 00:09:59 Priya: noted. thanks everyone, we’ll follow up after the benchmarks 00:10:03 Recording: meeting ended 55 min 00:10:08 [end of transcript]
